title: Peer review and how journals work
note: In peer review, an editor sends a manuscript to independent experts, whose reports guide the editor's decision. It filters out much weak work but does not prove a result true. Journal metrics such as the impact factor are rough signals about a journal, never verdicts on a single article.

read.title: What a journal adds
text: When researchers finish a study, they submit a manuscript to a journal. An editor first decides whether it fits the journal and is worth reviewing; many papers are declined at this stage. The rest go to two or three independent experts who judge whether the methods are sound, the analysis fits the data, and the conclusions follow. Their reports guide the editor, who may accept, reject, or ask for revisions.

This filter is valuable but limited. Reviewers rarely see raw data, so plausible fabrication can slip through, and honest errors survive too. Peer review means a paper was checked by experts, not that its conclusions are true.

Readers often judge journals by the impact factor, the average number of citations a journal's recent articles receive. It is a rough signal at best. A few blockbuster papers can lift the average, fields cite at very different rates, and it says nothing about any one article.

The worst outlets imitate journals without doing the work. Predatory journals collect publication fees while skipping real review. Spam invitations, promises of acceptance in days, and editorial boards that can't be verified are warning signs.
